title: Lemon Delicious Pudding
subtitle: Self-saucing baked pudding: soft sponge top, lemon sauce underneath
excerpt: A single batter that separates in the oven into a light, set sponge on top and a sharp, curd-like lemon sauce beneath, served from the dish so both layers reach the plate together.
sourceNotes: An Australian and British favourite since the mid-20th century. The chemistry of the self-saucing effect relies on the beaten egg whites rising while the heavier lemon-milk base sinks to form the sauce. The bain-marie is what makes this possible, it prevents the bottom from curdling before the top has set.

content.text: Lemon delicious pudding is a self-saucing baked dessert: beaten eggs, lemon, flour, and milk go in as one batter, and during the oven the sponge rises while the lemon sauce forms underneath. The contrast between the airy, set sponge on top and the sharp, curd-like sauce below is the entire point of the pudding. Bake at 180°C in a bain-marie for 35 to 40 minutes, the water bath is not optional, as it keeps the sauce from over-cooking.

Preheat the oven to 180°C. Grease a 1.2-litre baking dish. Separate the eggs, placing the whites in a clean, grease-free bowl and the yolks in a larger bowl. Have a roasting tin ready that the baking dish will sit inside.

Beat the butter and sugar together until pale and creamy. Beat in the egg yolks one at a time. Stir in the lemon zest, then the lemon juice, the mixture may look curdled at this stage, which is fine. Fold in the flour, then gradually stir in the milk to give a smooth, thin batter.

Whisk the egg whites in a clean bowl to stiff peaks, they should hold their shape and not slide when the bowl is tilted. Add one large spoonful of whites to the lemon batter and stir in to loosen it slightly. Fold in the remaining whites in two batches, using a large metal spoon and a gentle, sweeping motion. Stop folding while streaks of white are still just visible, over-folding deflates the whites and the sponge will not rise.

Pour the batter into the greased baking dish. Place the dish inside the roasting tin. Carefully pour enough boiling water into the roasting tin to come halfway up the outside of the baking dish. Slide into the oven and bake for 35 to 40 minutes until the top is set and lightly golden and has a faint spring when touched. The bain-marie water should be simmering gently throughout.
Serve immediately from the dish, using a large spoon to scoop through both the sponge and the sauce below. Dust with icing sugar if you like, and serve with cream or ice cream alongside.

items.symptom: No sauce has formed, the whole thing is sponge
items.cause: The bain-marie was dry, or the oven temperature was too high, cooking the base before it could separate.
items.fix: Check that the roasting tin had enough water and that it was simmering throughout. Ensure the oven is not running significantly hot.

items.symptom: The sponge is dense and did not rise
items.cause: The egg whites were over-folded, deflating the air beaten into them.
items.fix: Fold more gently and stop sooner, a few streaks of white in the batter is correct. The batter should feel airy and light when it goes into the dish.

items.cause: Too much lemon juice, or very large sharp lemons were used.
items.fix: Use 2 medium lemons and taste the batter before adding the egg whites, adjust sugar if needed.

content.text: Best eaten immediately, straight from the oven, while the layers are distinct. Leftovers can be refrigerated for 1 day but the sponge absorbs the sauce overnight and the layers merge. Still pleasant cold, but a different thing.
